explanation.text:
(Pro. 26:1-28)

The incongruities of nature illustrate also those of the moral world. The fool's unworthiness is also implied (Pro 17:7; Pro 19:10).

bsb.text: Like snow in summer and rain at harvest, honor does not befit a fool.

explanation.text:
Though not obvious to us,

the bird--literally, "sparrow"--and

swallow--have an object in their motions, so penal evil falls on none without a reason.

bsb.text: Like a fluttering sparrow or darting swallow, an undeserved curse does not come to rest.

explanation.text: The rod is as much needed by fools and as well suited to them, as whips and bridles are for beasts.

bsb.text: A whip for the horse, a bridle for the donkey, and a rod for the backs of fools!

explanation.text: Answer not--that is, approvingly by like folly.

bsb.text: Do not answer a fool according to his folly, or you yourself will be like him.

explanation.text: Answer--by reproof.

bsb.text: Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he become wise in his own eyes.

explanation.text:
A fool fails by folly as surely as if he were maimed.

drinketh damage--that is, gets it abundantly (Job 15:16; Job 34:7).

bsb.text: Like cutting off one’s own feet or drinking violence is the sending of a message by the hand of a fool.

explanation.text: legs . . . equal--or, "take away the legs," or "the legs . . . are weak." In any case the idea is that they are the occasion of an awkwardness, such as the fool shows in using a parable or proverb (see Introduction; Pro 17:7).

bsb.text: Like lame legs hanging limp is a proverb in the mouth of a fool.

explanation.text: A stone, bound in a sling, is useless; so honor, conferred on a fool, is thrown away.

bsb.text: Like binding a stone into a sling is the giving of honor to a fool.

explanation.text: As vexatious and unmanageable as a thorn in a drunkard's hand is a parable to a fool. He will be as apt to misuse is as to use it rightly.

bsb.text: Like a thorn that goes into the hand of a drunkard is a proverb in the mouth of a fool.

explanation.text:
Various versions of this are proposed (compare Margin). Better perhaps--"Much He injures (or literally, "wounds") all who reward," etc., that is, society is injured by encouraging evil men.

transgressors--may be rendered "vagrants." The word "God" is improperly supplied.

bsb.text: Like an archer who wounds at random is he who hires a fool or passerby.

explanation.text: returneth . . . folly--Though disgusting to others, the fool delights in his folly.

bsb.text: As a dog returns to its vomit, so a fool repeats his folly.

explanation.text: The self-conceited are taught with more difficulty than the stupid.

bsb.text: Do you see a man who is wise in his own eyes? There is more hope for a fool than for him.

explanation.text: (Compare Pro 22:13).

bsb.text: The slacker says, “A lion is in the road! A fierce lion roams the public square!”

explanation.text: (Compare Pro 6:10; Pro 24:33).

bsb.text: As a door turns on its hinges, so the slacker turns on his bed.

explanation.text: (Compare Pro 19:24).

bsb.text: The slacker buries his hand in the dish; it wearies him to bring it back to his mouth.

explanation.text: The thoughtless being ignorant of their ignorance are conceited.

bsb.text: The slacker is wiser in his own eyes than seven men who answer discreetly.

explanation.text: meddleth--as in Pro 20:19; Pro 24:21; as either holding a dog by the ears or letting him go involves danger, so success in another man's strife or failure involves a useless risk of reputation, does no good, and may do us harm.

bsb.text: Like one who grabs a dog by the ears is a passerby who meddles in a quarrel not his own.

explanation.text: Such are reckless of results.

bsb.text: Like a madman shooting firebrands and deadly arrows,

explanation.text:
So is the man that deceiveth his neighbour,.... By telling him a lie; or by reporting false things concerning him; or by cheating him in trade and commerce; or by taking his goods privately from him; and, when caught in either of these,

and saith, Am not I in sport? do not be angry, I designed no hurt; it is all in jest, a mere joke: but, had he not been apprehended, it would have been in earnest, as he was. This is only an excuse, and as absurd an one as if a man should set fire to his neighbour's house and barns, or throw arrows at him, or strike him with any instrument of death, as the sword, etc. and then say he was only in jest, or pretend madness.

bsb.text: so is the man who deceives his neighbor and says, “I was only joking!”

explanation.text: The talebearers foster (Pro 16:28), and the contentious excite, strife.

bsb.text: Without wood, a fire goes out; without gossip, a conflict ceases.

explanation.text:
As coals are to burning coals, and wood to fire,.... As brands, wood half burnt, or dead coals put to live and burning ones, soon take fire and become like them, and fit and proper fuel for them, and add to their heat:

so is a contentious man to kindle strife; or "a man of contentions"; who is given to it, is full of it; it is agreeable to his natural temper and disposition; he is in his element when at it; such a man is as fuel to the fire, as a dead coal to a living one, which increases the heat of it; so does he, he kindles and spreads the flame of contention and strife.

bsb.text: Like charcoal for embers and wood for fire, so is a quarrelsome man for kindling strife.

explanation.text: (Compare Pro 18:8).

bsb.text: The words of a gossip are like choice morsels that go down into the inmost being.

explanation.text: Warm professions can no more give value to insincerity than silver coating to rude earthenware.

bsb.text: Like glaze covering an earthen vessel are burning lips and a wicked heart.

explanation.text: dissembleth--though an unusual sense of the word (compare Margin), is allowable, and better suits the context, which sets forth hypocrisy.

bsb.text: A hateful man disguises himself with his speech, but he lays up deceit in his heart.

explanation.text:
Sentiment of Pro 26:24 carried out.

seven abominations in his heart--that is, very many (compare Pro 24:16).

bsb.text: When he speaks graciously, do not believe him, for seven abominations fill his heart.

explanation.text: Deceit will at last be exposed, and the wicked by their own arts often bring on retribution (compare Pro 12:13; Psa 7:16; Psa 9:17, etc.).

bsb.text: Though his hatred is concealed by deception, his wickedness will be exposed in the assembly.

explanation.text:
Whoso diggeth a pit shall fall therein,.... That devises mischief against others, it shall come upon himself. The allusion is to the digging of pits for catching wild beasts, which are slightly covered with earth; and which sometimes the pursuers, through inadvertency, fall into themselves; the passage seems to be taken from Psalm 7:15;

and he that rolleth a stone, it will return upon him; that rolls a stone up hill, if he does not take care, it will return back, and fall with great force upon himself; so the mischief which a wicked man labours hard at, as men do in digging a pit, or rolling a stone, in time rolls back upon themselves; the measure they mete out to others is measured to them. Jarchi makes mention of an "hagadah", or exposition, which illustrates this passage, by the case of Abimelech; who slew threescore and ten persons on one stone, and was himself killed with a piece of a millstone cast upon him, Judges 9:18; this may put in mind of the fable of Sisyphus, feigned in hell to roll a great stone to the top of a mountain, which presently falling down on his head, made his labour fruitless.

bsb.text: He who digs a pit will fall into it, and he who rolls a stone will have it roll back on him.

explanation.text:
Men hate those they injure.

A lying tongue--"lips" for the persons (compare Pro 4:24; Psa 12:3).

Next: Proverbs Chapter 27

bsb.text: A lying tongue hates those it crushes, and a flattering mouth causes ruin.
